tagline: Oñate's road north, across the dead man's ninety miles.
intro: The byway starts at Fort Selden, twelve miles north of Las Cruces, where the old road left the Rio Grande. Ahead lies the Jornada del Muerto, a flat desert basin with mountains on the west shutting off the river and an almost waterless 90 miles of trail across it. South of Socorro the road comes back to the valley and follows it north through Albuquerque and Santa Fe to Ohkay Owingeh.
Juan de Oñate led 500 colonists up this way in 1598. The road stayed in use until 1882, the northern end of a royal road that began at a plaza in Mexico City.

moments.title: Fort Selden
moments.text: Before the fort this was Paraje de Robledo, the last camp on the river before the Jornada, named for a soldier of Oñate's who died in 1598 and was buried here under a cross.

moments.title: Socorro
moments.text: Coming out of the Jornada in June 1598, Oñate's party was given food and water by the Piro people of Teypana pueblo, and called the place Socorro, which means help.

moments.title: Ohkay Owingeh
moments.text: The end of the road. Oñate arrived on July 11, 1598, and made it the province's first capital until 1610. In 2005 the pueblo took back its own name, place of the Strong People.
